passages.text: METEORS, in physiology, are the various appearances in the air, whether watery, as rain, hail, and snow; or fiery, as lightning, fire-balls, and shooting stars.
Shooting stars are supposed to be small portions of inflammable vapour, raised from the earth, which take fire in the upper air and are quickly consumed.
Fire-balls are larger, and have been seen to pass over whole countries at the height of many miles, sometimes bursting with a noise like cannon.

It has been reported that stones have fallen from the sky, accompanied by such meteors; but these accounts are generally disbelieved by philosophers, and the stones are thought to have been struck by lightning or thrown up by volcanoes.
Mr Chladni has lately maintained that fire-balls are masses of matter from beyond the atmosphere, which take fire on entering it; but this opinion is thought extravagant.

A meteoroid is a small rocky or metallic body travelling through space. When it enters Earth's atmosphere at high speed it heats up and glows, producing a streak of light called a meteor, or shooting star.
Most meteors come from particles no bigger than a grain of sand and burn up completely at heights of about 75 to 120 kilometres.
A very bright meteor is called a fireball or bolide; some explode in the air, and their sound can be heard on the ground.
A meteoroid that survives its passage and lands on the ground is called a meteorite.
In 1794 Ernst Chladni argued that meteorites came from space. The idea was widely rejected until a shower of stones fell at L'Aigle in France in 1803 and was investigated by Jean-Baptiste Biot.
Meteor showers, such as the Perseids, occur when the Earth passes through streams of debris left by comets.
The word meteor comes from the Greek meteoros, 'high in the air'.

reasons: In 1797 METEORS covered rain, snow and lightning as well as shooting stars, so no single Wikipedia article matches the whole entry.

alignments.label: What a meteor is

britannica.quote: the various appearances in the air, whether watery, as rain, hail, and snow

wikipedia.quote: The word meteor comes from the Greek meteoros, 'high in the air'

alignments.note: A change in language: in 1797 rain and snow were meteors. Today only the fiery kind keeps the name.

alignments.label: Shooting stars

britannica.quote: small portions of inflammable vapour, raised from the earth, which take fire in the upper air

wikipedia.quote: When it enters Earth's atmosphere at high speed it heats up and glows

alignments.note: Right that they burn high in the air. They come from space, not from the earth.

alignments.label: Bursting fire-balls

britannica.quote: sometimes bursting with a noise like cannon

wikipedia.quote: some explode in the air, and their sound can be heard on the ground

alignments.note: Same event, described the same way.

alignments.label: Stones from the sky

britannica.quote: these accounts are generally disbelieved by philosophers

wikipedia.quote: A meteoroid that survives its passage and lands on the ground is called a meteorite

alignments.note: The witnesses were right and the philosophers wrong. Stones do fall from the sky.

alignments.label: Chladni

britannica.quote: masses of matter from beyond the atmosphere, which take fire on entering it

wikipedia.quote: In 1794 Ernst Chladni argued that meteorites came from space

alignments.note: The view the 1797 entry calls extravagant was proved six years later, at L'Aigle.

alignments.label: Meteor showers

wikipedia.quote: streams of debris left by comets

alignments.note: The link between comets and shooting stars was made in the 1860s.

suggestedQuestions: Did people in 1797 believe stones could fall from the sky?

Did people in 1797 believe stones could.answer: Mostly not. The 1797 entry says such reports were generally disbelieved, and the stones thought to be struck by lightning or thrown up by volcanoes [B4]. Wikipedia says stones that survive their fall are meteorites [W4], and that the question was settled by the shower of stones at L'Aigle in 1803 [W5].

Was Chladni right about fire-balls?.answer: Yes. The 1797 entry reports his view that fire-balls are masses from beyond the atmosphere that take fire on entering it, and calls it extravagant [B5]. Wikipedia says Chladni argued in 1794 that meteorites came from space, and that the idea was accepted after L'Aigle in 1803 [W5].
